title: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
summary: What -O levels switch on, the passes behind them, why inlining and vectorization matter, how UB changes results at -O2, LTO, PGO and how to measure.
outcomes: Explain why -O0 code keeps every variable in memory and what bundles -O1, -O2, -O3, -Os, -Og and -Ofast enable
Read LLVM IR in SSA form and name the passes (mem2reg, constant propagation, CSE, LICM) that turn -O0 code into -O2 code
Trace how inlining enables constant folding, and why it cannot cross .c files or exported .so symbols without help
Predict whether GCC vectorizes a loop at -O2 or -O3 given its trip count and pointer aliasing
Explain how -O2 exploits undefined behavior (overflow, strict aliasing, null checks) and debug a bug that appears only at -O2

blocks.md:
You compile the same C file twice, once with `-O0` and once with `-O2`, and one binary runs several times faster. Nothing in your algorithm changed. What changed is how much freedom you gave the compiler to rewrite your program, as long as the visible result stays the same.

This course is about that freedom: what the levels turn on, the three transformations that matter most (**inlining**, **vectorization**, **link-time optimization**), and the flags that buy speed at a price.

Start with the default. This course uses two C compilers: GCC, whose C compiler is the `gcc` command, and Clang, the C compiler built on the LLVM compiler toolkit (LLVM once stood for Low Level Virtual Machine; today it is just the project's name). GCC's manual says that without optimization the goal is fast compiles and predictable debugging: *statements are independent*, so you can stop at a breakpoint, change any variable, and the program continues exactly as the source says. To make that true, the compiler keeps every variable in its stack slot and reloads it at each statement.

The listings are x86-64 assembly: the 64-bit version of the x86 instruction family that Intel and AMD processors run. They use Intel syntax, which writes the destination first, so `add rax, rdx` means rax = rax + rdx, and square brackets mean the memory at that address. gcc prints the reverse order, AT&T syntax, unless you pass `-masm=intel`.

blocks.caption: We compile this with GCC 14 for x86-64 Linux and print Intel-syntax assembly with -S -masm=intel.

blocks.title: The same loop at -O0 and at -O2 (x86-64, GCC)
blocks.code:
; gcc -O0 (Intel syntax)
sum:
  push rbp
  mov  rbp, rsp
  mov  QWORD PTR [rbp-24], rdi   ; a to stack
  mov  QWORD PTR [rbp-32], rsi   ; n to stack
  mov  QWORD PTR [rbp-8], 0      ; s = 0
  mov  QWORD PTR [rbp-16], 0     ; i = 0
  jmp  .L2
.L3:
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-16]   ; load i
  lea  rdx, [0+rax*8]
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-24]   ; load a
  add  rax, rdx
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rax]      ; load a[i]
  add  QWORD PTR [rbp-8], rax    ; s += (load+store)
  add  QWORD PTR [rbp-16], 1     ; i++ (load+store)
.L2:
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-16]   ; load i
  cmp  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-32]   ; load n
  jl   .L3
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-8]
  pop  rbp
  ret
; gcc -O2
sum:
  test rsi, rsi                  ; n <= 0?
  jle  .L4
  lea  rdx, [rdi+rsi*8]          ; end = a + n
  xor  eax, eax                  ; s = 0 (in rax)
.L3:
  add  rax, QWORD PTR [rdi]      ; s += *p
  add  rdi, 8                    ; p++
  cmp  rdi, rdx
  jne  .L3
  ret
.L4:
  xor  eax, eax
  ret

scenes.caption: At -O0 the first thing sum does is copy its arguments a and n from registers into stack slots, and give s and i stack slots too. Every variable now lives in memory.
One trip through the -O0 loop: 10 instructions, 7 memory loads and 2 stores, to do one addition. i and s are reloaded from memory every time because the compiler keeps each statement independent.
At -O2, s stays in register rax and the index is replaced by a pointer that walks the array. The loop is 4 instructions with a single load. Lesson 2 names the passes that do this.
For n = 1000 that is 10013 instructions at -O0 versus 4005 at -O2. Nothing about the algorithm changed, only how much the compiler was allowed to assume.

blocks.md: An **optimization level** is not one magic switch. It is a named bundle of individual **passes**. A pass is one sweep of the compiler over a function that applies one kind of rewrite, and each has its own `-f` flag: `-ftree-dce` (dead code elimination, which deletes computations whose results are never used), `-finline-small-functions`, `-ftree-loop-vectorize` and so on. Each level turns on everything the previous one did plus more. Run `gcc -Q --help=optimizers -O2` to print the exact set your build of GCC enables, since it varies a little by target.

blocks.title: How GCC's optimization levels relate

scenes.caption: -O0 is the default. GCC disables most optimization passes here, even ones you request with -f flags, so that the code matches the source line by line.
-O1, -O2 and -O3 are cumulative bundles. GCC's manual lists about 48 flags for -O1, about 55 more for -O2 and 12 more for -O3; the lists change a little with each release.

-O2 is the usual release level: nearly every optimization without a space-speed tradeoff. -O3 adds loop transforms and a more willing vectorizer, the pass that makes one instruction work on several array elements at once.
Side branches: -Og is -O1 minus passes that hurt debugging, -Os is -O2 minus passes that grow code, and -Oz trades even more speed for bytes.
-Ofast is -O3 plus -ffast-math and other options that are not valid for every standards-conforming program. It can change your results.

blocks.md:
The variants, as GCC's manual defines them:

- `-O1` (same as `-O`): cheap optimizations that do not take a lot of compile time.
- `-O2`: nearly all optimizations that do not trade space for speed.
- `-O3`: adds loop transforms such as `-funswitch-loops` (when an `if` inside a loop tests something the loop never changes, make two copies of the loop and choose one before entering it) and `-fpeel-loops` (run the first few trips of a short loop as straight-line code, or write out a loop with a small constant count completely), plus a vectorizer cost model that accepts runtime checks. The cost model is the rule that decides whether vectorizing a loop pays off (lesson 4).
- `-Os` and `-Oz`: optimize for size. `-Og`: optimize but keep the debugging experience.
- `-Ofast`: `-O3` plus `-ffast-math`, which lets the compiler ignore strict floating-point rules (lesson 7), and other rule-bending options.

The other compiler, Clang, accepts the same spellings with similar meanings.

blocks.title: sum(a, 1000) compiled at each level (x86-64, GCC)

scenes.caption: Instructions executed for n = 1000, counted from each listing: a proxy for speed, not a timing (lesson 8 measures time). -O3 wins because it vectorizes the loop (lesson 4); -Os executes more than -O2 because it chose a smaller loop shape.
Size of the sum function in bytes. -O3 is 3x bigger than -O2 (setup and cleanup code around the vector loop) and -Os is the smallest. Speed and size pull in different directions.

blocks.prompt: You compile with `gcc -O2 -O0 file.c` because a Makefile appends flags. Which level is used?
blocks.reveal: **-O0.** GCC's manual says that with multiple `-O` options the *last* one wins. This is a classic reason a benchmark build is mysteriously slow: some later variable in the build system appended `-O0` or `-Og`. Check the actual compile command, not the one you think you wrote.

blocks.md: Misconception: "-O3 is always faster than -O2." -O3 makes code bigger and adds transforms that only pay off for some loops. Bigger code can cost instruction-cache misses: the instruction cache is a small, fast memory next to the core (typically tens of kilobytes) that holds recently run machine code, and code that does not fit there must be fetched from slower memory. Measure both on your workload; -O2 is the common default for release builds.

An -O level is a bundle of passes. -O0 keeps every variable in memory for debuggability; -O2 is the standard speed level; -O3, -Os, -Og and -Ofast each trade something (size, speed, debuggability, strictness) for something else.

blocks.question: In the -O0 listing, why does the loop reload `i` from the stack every iteration even though it just stored it?
options: The -O0 contract keeps statements independent so a debugger can change i between them
The CPU requires a load before every add
The register file is too small to hold i
-O0 does not know how to use registers at all
blocks.explain: At -O0 GCC promises that stopping between statements and editing a variable works as the source says. So each statement reads its inputs from memory and writes results back. Registers are used, but only briefly within one statement.

blocks.question: You ship firmware into a 32 KB flash chip and the hot path is not performance critical. Which level fits best?
blocks.explain: -Os enables the -O2 passes except those that often grow code, and -Oz goes further. In the measured sum function -Os produced 22 bytes versus 35 at -O2 and 105 at -O3. -O0 is both big and slow.

lessons.title: Inside the optimizer: IR, SSA and the classic scalar passes

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 showed `sum` shrinking from a 10-instruction loop at -O0 to 4 instructions at -O2, and put it down to how much the compiler was allowed to assume. This lesson opens the box and names the rewrites that did it.

Start tiny. Nobody writes `int m = 4 * 2;` on purpose, but after inlining and macro expansion, code like that is everywhere. A compiler that turns `m` into 8 once, and then reuses that fact in every later rewrite, is doing what all of -O2 does: many small rewrites, each provably safe, each one exposing the next.

A modern compiler has three parts. The **front end** parses C, checks types and reports errors. It then lowers the program into an **intermediate representation (IR)**: the compiler's own simple, explicit language between C and machine code. The **middle end**, the optimizer, runs **passes** that each read IR and write better IR, mostly without caring which CPU you target. The **back end** turns IR into instructions for one target.

Clang's IR is LLVM IR; GCC's main one is called GIMPLE. Because passes only speak IR, one optimizer serves many languages: rustc, the Rust compiler, also hands its code to LLVM.

blocks.title: From C source to assembly: front end, optimizer, back end

nodes.label:
optimizer passes
mem2reg, sccp, gvn, licm

scenes.caption: The front end parses and type-checks one translation unit and lowers it to IR. At this point every C variable still has its own memory slot.
The optimizer is a list of passes. Each reads IR and writes IR, so passes can run in any order and some run several times. An -O level mostly chooses which passes run.
The back end selects real instructions, assigns values to the CPU's registers and orders the instructions, then writes assembly.
At -O0 Clang tags every function optnone, which the LLVM manual says makes most passes skip it. The pipeline still runs; the rewrites do not.

blocks.md:
See it yourself: `clang -O0 -S -emit-llvm sum.c` writes the LLVM IR of lesson 1's `sum` to `sum.ll`. At -O0 Clang gives every C variable a stack slot with `alloca`, turns every read into a `load` and every write into a `store`: the same memory traffic as lesson 1's -O0 assembly.

Reading it: names that start with `%` are local values, which the reference manual calls register names (they are not the CPU's registers). `i64` is a 64-bit integer, `icmp slt` is a signed less-than compare, `getelementptr` computes an element's address from a pointer and an index without touching memory, `br` is a branch, and each `name:` label starts a **basic block**, a straight run of instructions entered only at the top.

blocks.title: The sum loop in LLVM IR, before and after mem2reg
blocks.code:
; clang -O0 -S -emit-llvm (loop only, trimmed)
for.cond:
  %0 = load i64, ptr %i
  %1 = load i64, ptr %n.addr
  %cmp = icmp slt i64 %0, %1
  br i1 %cmp, label %for.body, label %for.end
for.body:
  %2 = load ptr, ptr %a.addr
  %3 = load i64, ptr %i
  %arrayidx = getelementptr inbounds i64, ptr %2, i64 %3
  %4 = load i64, ptr %arrayidx
  %5 = load i64, ptr %s
  %add = add nsw i64 %5, %4
  store i64 %add, ptr %s
  br label %for.inc
for.inc:
  %6 = load i64, ptr %i
  %inc = add nsw i64 %6, 1
  store i64 %inc, ptr %i
  br label %for.cond
; after opt -passes=mem2reg
for.cond:
  %s.0 = phi i64 [ 0, %entry ], [ %add, %for.inc ]
  %i.0 = phi i64 [ 0, %entry ], [ %inc, %for.inc ]
  %cmp = icmp slt i64 %i.0, %n
  br i1 %cmp, label %for.body, label %for.end
for.body:
  %arrayidx = getelementptr inbounds i64, ptr %a, i64 %i.0
  %0 = load i64, ptr %arrayidx
  %add = add nsw i64 %s.0, %0
  br label %for.inc
for.inc:
  %inc = add nsw i64 %i.0, 1
  br label %for.cond
for.end:
  ret i64 %s.0

scenes.caption: At -O0 each trip loads i and n from their slots just to compare them. Count the whole loop: 7 loads and 2 stores per element, the same as lesson 1's -O0 assembly.
The body reloads a, i and s, adds, and stores s back; the increment block reloads i and stores it again.
mem2reg (promote memory to register) deletes the slots. A variable that changes around the loop becomes a phi at the loop head: %s.0 and %i.0.
Now the only load is a[i] itself, and s never touches memory. That is the first step toward lesson 1's -O2 loop that keeps s in rax.

blocks.md:
The mem2reg output is in **static single assignment (SSA)** form, which the LLVM reference manual names as the basis of LLVM IR: every value is assigned in exactly one place in the code and never changes afterwards. A C variable that changes, like `s`, becomes several values (`%s.0`, `%add`).

Where control flow merges, a **phi** instruction picks the value that matches the block execution came from. `%s.0 = phi i64 [ 0, %entry ], [ %add, %for.inc ]` means: 0 when arriving from `entry`, `%add` when arriving from the loop body. LLVM's pass list describes mem2reg as the standard SSA construction algorithm. One definition per value is what makes later passes cheap: to learn where `%add` came from, a pass reads one instruction instead of hunting for every store that might have changed `s`.

blocks.prompt: In SSA every value is assigned exactly once. Yet the loop counter takes the values 0, 1, 2 and so on. How can `%i.0` be a single value?
blocks.reveal: Single assignment is about the program text, not about time. `%i.0` has one definition, the phi at the loop head, and that one instruction runs again on every trip. Each time it picks 0 if execution came from `entry`, or `%inc` (which is `%i.0 + 1`) if it came back around the loop. So one definition produces a new value per trip, and no instruction ever overwrites another's result.

blocks.md:
Now four classic passes on a small function. Each is a separate LLVM pass you can run alone with `opt -passes=<name>` (opt is LLVM's standalone optimizer), and GCC's manual lists its own versions:

- **Constant propagation** replaces values known at compile time with constants: LLVM `sccp` (sparse conditional constant propagation), GCC `-ftree-ccp`.
- **Dead code elimination (DCE)** deletes computations whose results nobody uses: LLVM `dce`, GCC `-ftree-dce`.
- **Common subexpression elimination (CSE)** computes a repeated expression once: LLVM `gvn` (global value numbering), GCC `-ftree-fre` (full redundancy elimination).
- **Instruction combining** rewrites short sequences into simpler ones: LLVM `instcombine`, which its docs call the place where algebraic simplification happens.

blocks.caption: Compiled with clang -O0 -Xclang -disable-O0-optnone -S -emit-llvm, then run through opt one pass at a time (LLVM 22). Every listing below is real opt output, trimmed to the function body. A release build of clang numbers the values (%2, %3); add -fno-discard-value-names to see the names shown.

blocks.title: One function, one pass at a time (LLVM IR)
blocks.code:
; after mem2reg
  %mul = mul nsw i32 4, 2
  %mul1 = mul nsw i32 %x, %mul
  %mul2 = mul nsw i32 %x, %mul
  %sub = sub nsw i32 %mul1, 1
  %add = add nsw i32 %mul1, %mul2
  ret i32 %add
; after sccp (constant propagation)
  %mul1 = mul nsw i32 %x, 8
  %mul2 = mul nsw i32 %x, 8
  %sub = sub nsw i32 %mul1, 1
  %add = add nsw i32 %mul1, %mul2
  ret i32 %add
; after dce
  %mul1 = mul nsw i32 %x, 8
  %mul2 = mul nsw i32 %x, 8
  %add = add nsw i32 %mul1, %mul2
  ret i32 %add
; after gvn (common subexpressions)
  %mul1 = mul nsw i32 %x, 8
  %add = add nsw i32 %mul1, %mul1
  ret i32 %add
; after instcombine
  %add = shl nsw i32 %x, 4
  ret i32 %add
; x86-64 assembly at -O2 (clang; gcc prints sal)
  mov  eax, edi
  shl  eax, 4
  ret

scenes.caption: After mem2reg the six stack slots are gone. nsw means no signed wrap: the manual makes the result poison (invalid) on signed overflow. Clang marks signed int math this way because C leaves that overflow undefined (lesson 5).
sccp: 4 x 2 is known at compile time, so it becomes 8 and is used directly. LLVM's docs note this pass tends to leave dead definitions behind and suggest a DCE pass after it.
dce: %sub (the variable unused) feeds nothing, so it is deleted.
gvn: %mul2 computes exactly what %mul1 computes, so its uses are rewired to %mul1 and it disappears.
instcombine: x * 8 + x * 8 is x * 16, and multiplying by 16 is a left shift by 4.
The back end emits 3 instructions. Clang -O2 runs all of these passes (and many more) in its own order; GCC reaches the same code with its own passes.

blocks.md:
Loops are where the time goes, so two loop passes matter most.

- **Loop-invariant code motion (LICM)** moves a computation whose inputs do not change inside the loop to the block just before it, the **preheader**, so it runs once instead of every trip. LLVM's pass is `licm`; GCC's is loop invariant motion, `-ftree-loop-im`.
- **Strength reduction** replaces an expensive operation on the loop counter with a cheaper running update: instead of computing `i * c` each trip, add `c` to a running value. A value that changes by a fixed step every trip, like `i`, is an **induction variable**. GCC's `-fivopts` performs strength reduction, induction variable merging and induction variable elimination; LLVM's `loop-reduce` does this for array addresses.

blocks.caption: The GIMPLE below is from GCC 14's -fdump-tree-optimized on an AArch64 build; the x86-64 assembly from GCC 14 on Compiler Explorer makes the same choices. In the dump, <bb N> is basic block N, names like _7 are SSA values, and MEM[...] = is a store.

blocks.title: LICM and strength reduction in GCC's GIMPLE and assembly

scenes.caption: LICM: k * 4 does not change inside the loop, so it sits in bb 3, the preheader that runs once. k_10(D) is an SSA version of k; GCC prints (D) for a default definition, here the value k has on entry.
GIMPLE is SSA too: the # PHI lines are phi nodes. Strength reduction: there is no i * (k * 4) anywhere. ivtmp.8 starts at 0 and gains _15 (k * 4) each trip.
The index i is gone as well. ivtmp.9 is the address itself, starting at a and stepping by 8 bytes, and the loop ends when it reaches _27, which is a + n * 8.
The same plan in x86-64: one shift before the loop, then 5 instructions per element. Lesson 1's sum loop, with its walking pointer in rdi, came from this same pass.

blocks.md:
The back end finishes the job. **Instruction selection** picks real instructions for each IR operation: `shl` for a multiply by 16, or an address like `[rdi+rsi*8]` that folds a multiply and an add into one operand. **Register allocation** maps the unlimited SSA values onto the CPU's few registers and spills a value to a stack slot only when they run out; GCC's allocator is called IRA, the integrated register allocator. **Instruction scheduling** reorders instructions so the CPU is not left waiting for data that is not ready yet.

So lesson 1's -O2 `sum` keeps `s` in `rax` because mem2reg (in GCC, its own SSA construction) turned `s` into a value and the allocator found a register for it, and its walking pointer came from induction variable optimization.

To watch passes on your own code:

- `clang -O0 -Xclang -disable-O0-optnone -S -emit-llvm f.c`, then `opt -S -passes=mem2reg,sccp f.ll`. The extra flag matters: without it every function carries `optnone` and the passes skip it.
- `gcc -O2 -fdump-tree-all f.c` turns on every GIMPLE dump, one file per pass (the final optimized GIMPLE is `f.c.*t.optimized`), and `-fdump-passes` prints which passes are on.
- [Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org) compiles in the browser with many compilers and flags side by side; the assembly listings in this course were checked there.

Misconception: "the optimizer understands what my code is for." It does not. Each pass applies one local rewrite it can prove safe, and the big wins come from chains: inlining exposes a constant, propagation folds it, DCE deletes the leftovers. When a chain breaks (a call it cannot see into, a pointer that might alias), every later step is lost.

Compilers optimize an IR in SSA form: one definition per value, with phi nodes where paths merge. mem2reg takes variables out of memory; constant propagation, DCE and CSE simplify straight-line code; LICM and strength reduction slim loops; the back end selects instructions, allocates registers and schedules.

blocks.question: In lesson 1's -O0 listing, sum loads and stores s on every trip. Which steps remove that memory traffic at -O2?
options: Promoting the stack slot to an SSA value (mem2reg), then register allocation
blocks.explain: The traffic exists because s has a stack slot. mem2reg replaces the slot's loads and stores with SSA values and a phi, and the register allocator then keeps that value in rax. LICM moves invariant work, but s changes every trip; DCE deletes unused work, but s is used.

blocks.question: A loop runs n times and computes `x / d` on every trip; x and d never change inside it. Why can't the compiler simply move the division above the loop?
options: If n is 0 the original never divides, but the moved division would run, and divide by zero if d is 0
Integer division gives a different result outside a loop
LICM only moves loads, never arithmetic
Divisions are too slow to move
blocks.explain: A rewrite must not add behavior the original never had. With n = 0 and d = 0 the source is fine, but a division placed before the loop would divide by zero, which is undefined and on x86-64 crashes. Compilers move such code only under the loop's entry test (like the n <= 0 check before ramp's loop) or leave it in place.

lessons.title: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization

blocks.md:
A function call has a direct cost: move arguments into registers as the application binary interface requires (the calling rules that say which registers carry arguments and results), execute `call` and `ret`, and set up and tear down a stack frame. For a tiny function that overhead can exceed the work itself.

The bigger cost is indirect. Most optimizations look at one function body at a time. Across a call boundary the compiler knows little about the callee, so it must assume the worst: the arguments could be anything and the callee might read or write memory.

**Inlining** replaces a call with a copy of the callee's body, with the parameters substituted by the actual arguments. GCC's manual puts it this way: besides removing call overhead, "if any of the actual argument values are constant, their known values may permit simplifications at compile time". Inlining is cheap by itself; its value is that it hands the next passes a bigger body with more facts in it.

blocks.code:
static int square(int x) { return x * x; }
int f(void) { return square(7) + 1; }
blocks.caption: Compiled at -O0 and at -O2 with GCC for x86-64.

blocks.title: Inlining square(7), then folding the constant

nodes.label:
static int square(int x)
return x * x;

scenes.caption: At -O0 f really calls square: it moves 7 into edi (the first argument register), executes call, and square sets up its own stack frame. 7 + 7 instructions to compute a constant.
Step 1, inline: the compiler copies square's body into f with x replaced by 7. The call, the argument move and square's frame setup all disappear.
Step 2, constant folding: 7 x 7 + 1 is known at compile time, so it becomes 50. This step was impossible before inlining because the compiler optimizes one function body at a time.
Final -O2 output: mov eax, 50 then ret. square was static and every call was inlined, so GCC does not emit it at all.

blocks.md:
Which calls get inlined is a heuristic decision, controlled by flags the levels turn on:

- `-finline-functions-called-once` (from -O1, not -Og): a `static` function with one call site is merged into its caller.
- `-finline-small-functions` (-O2): inline when the body is smaller than the call sequence, so code shrinks.
- `-finline-functions` (-O2, also enabled by `-fprofile-use`, the profile-guided build of lesson 7): consider every function and let a size and benefit estimate decide.

If all calls to a `static` function are inlined, no standalone copy is emitted.

The tradeoff is code size. Each inlined call site gets its own copy of the body. Inline a 40-instruction function at 50 call sites and you added about 2000 instructions, which can push hot code out of the instruction cache. GCC's manual says the effect of inlining on size "is less predictable": it may shrink or grow the program. This is one reason `-Os`, which tunes decisions for code size, inlines very differently from `-O3`.

Misconception: the `inline` keyword forces inlining. It is a hint plus linkage rules: rules about how the function's definition is shared between files. At -O2 the compiler inlines functions you never marked, and may refuse ones you did. At -O0 GCC inlines nothing unless the function has `__attribute__((always_inline))`.

blocks.prompt: Now move `square` into its own file `sq.c` (not static), keep only the declaration `int square(int x);` in the file with `f`, and compile each file with `gcc -O2 -c`. What does `f` compile to?
blocks.reveal:
A real call:

`sub rsp, 8` / `mov edi, 7` / `call square` / `add rsp, 8` / `add eax, 1` / `ret`

The `sub rsp, 8` and `add rsp, 8` only keep the stack 16-byte aligned at the call, as the application binary interface requires. The compiler sees one **translation unit** (one .c file after preprocessing) at a time. When it compiles f, square is only a declaration with no body, so there is nothing to inline and 50 cannot be computed. Lesson 6 fixes this with link-time optimization.

blocks.md: You can ask the compiler what it decided. GCC prints optimization remarks with `-fopt-info-inline` and Clang with `-Rpass=inline` (successes) or `-Rpass-missed=inline` (refusals). Reading these is faster than guessing from the assembly.

Shared libraries add a second wall. Code for a shared library is compiled with `-fPIC`, position-independent code that GCC's manual describes as suitable for dynamic linking. On ELF systems (ELF, the Executable and Linkable Format, is the file format Linux uses for programs and libraries) an exported function can then be **interposed**: the manual explains that the dynamic linker may substitute another definition of the symbol, so for exported functions the compiler cannot inline or propagate facts across the call, even within one file. `-fno-semantic-interposition` tells GCC to assume any substitute behaves the same, and `-fvisibility=hidden` stops exporting symbols by default, which the manual recommends for shared objects you distribute.

You can also steer single functions. `__attribute__((noinline))` keeps a function out of line, and `__attribute__((always_inline))` on an `inline` function inlines it regardless of the usual limits, with an error if that fails ([GCC function attributes](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Common-Attributes.html)).

blocks.prompt: Put this lesson's `square` and `f` in one file, with `square` not static, and compile it for a shared library with `gcc -O2 -fPIC`. Is `f` still `mov eax, 50`?
blocks.reveal:
**No.** GCC 14 emits `sub rsp, 8` / `mov edi, 7` / `call square@PLT` / `add rsp, 8` / `add eax, 1` / `ret`. The body of square is right there in the same file, but square is exported and could be interposed, so GCC must call whichever definition the dynamic linker picks, through the PLT (procedure linkage table), the stub table the dynamic linker fills in.

Add `-fno-semantic-interposition` or `-fvisibility=hidden` and f is `mov eax, 50` again. Clang 22 inlined it even with plain `-fPIC` in the same test, so check your own compiler's output.

blocks.md: Inlining matters less for the call it removes than for what it enables: constant folding, dead code removal and vectorization inside the merged body. It costs code size, and it only works when the callee's body is visible in the same compilation.

blocks.question: A hot loop calls `int clamp(int v)` defined in another .c file. Profiling shows the call overhead dominates. You compile with -O3. What happens?
options: -O3 inlines it because -O3 enables aggressive inlining
It stays a call: the body is in a different translation unit
It is inlined only if clamp is marked inline in its own .c file
blocks.explain: Inlining needs the callee's body. Without LTO each .c file is compiled alone, so no -O level can inline across files. Moving clamp into a header as static inline, or using -flto, makes the body visible.

blocks.question: Why can inlining make a program slower even though it removes call instructions?
options: Duplicated bodies grow the code and can cause instruction-cache misses
blocks.explain: Every call site gets its own copy. For large functions with many call sites, the bigger hot path may no longer fit in the instruction cache, and those misses can cost more than the calls saved. Compilers use size budgets for this reason.

lessons.title: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops

blocks.md:
Modern CPUs have **SIMD** (single instruction, multiple data) registers. On x86-64 the 128-bit `xmm` registers hold four 32-bit ints, and one `paddd` instruction (packed add of doublewords; Intel calls a 32-bit value a doubleword) adds four pairs at once. Each element slot of a vector register is called a **lane**. SSE2, short for Streaming SIMD Extensions 2, which provides them, is part of the baseline x86-64 target, so every x86-64 binary may use it.

**Auto-vectorization** is the compiler rewriting a scalar loop (one that handles one element per iteration) so each iteration processes several elements in SIMD lanes.

blocks.caption: Two versions of the same loop. restrict promises the compiler that the three arrays do not overlap.

blocks.title: a[i] = b[i] + c[i]: scalar steps versus 4-lane SIMD steps

scenes.caption: Scalar code (-O1): one load, one add and one store per element. Iteration 0 computes 3 + 2 = 5.
Iteration 1: 1 + 7 = 8. Eight elements need eight trips through the loop.
Vectorized (-O2 here): movdqu loads 16 bytes, that is four ints, from b and from c; paddd adds all four pairs in one instruction; movups stores four results.
Second vector iteration covers elements 4 to 7. Two trips instead of eight. For 1024 elements the loop runs 256 times instead of 1024.

blocks.code:
add_1024:            ; gcc -O2, x86-64
  xor  eax, eax
.L11:
  movdqu xmm0, XMMWORD PTR [rsi+rax]  ; 4 ints of b
  movdqu xmm1, XMMWORD PTR [rdx+rax]  ; 4 ints of c
  paddd  xmm0, xmm1                   ; 4 adds
  movups XMMWORD PTR [rdi+rax], xmm0  ; 4 ints of a
  add  rax, 16
  cmp  rax, 4096                      ; 1024 ints x 4 bytes
  jne  .L11
  ret
blocks.caption: The real vector loop GCC emits: 7 instructions per 4 elements.

blocks.md:
Vectorizing is only legal if it gives the same result as the scalar loop. Two things get in the way:

1. **Unknown trip count.** The trip count is how many times the loop body runs. If n is not a multiple of 4, a scalar **epilogue** loop must finish the last 1 to 3 elements.
2. **Possible aliasing.** Two pointers alias when they can reach the same memory. If `a` overlaps `b` or `c`, a store in one iteration can change what a later iteration reads. Then the compiler must add a **runtime check** and keep a scalar fallback, which is called *versioning* the loop.

blocks.prompt: Call the plain `add` with `b = {1,1,1,1,1}`, `c = {1,1,1,1}`, `a = b + 1` (so a[i] is b[i+1]) and n = 4. What does b hold after the scalar loop, and what would a naive 4-lane vector version produce?
blocks.reveal:
Scalar: each store feeds the next load. b[1] = 1 + 1 = 2, then b[2] = b[1] + 1 = 3, and so on, giving **b = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}**.

Naive vector: it loads b[0..3] = {1,1,1,1} *before* storing anything, adds 1, and writes {2,2,2,2}, giving **b = {1, 2, 2, 2, 2}**. Different answer, so the transformation is illegal for this overlap. GCC's -O3 code for `add` checks the pointer distance first and takes the scalar path when a starts 1 to 3 ints after b or c; a == b (in place) is safe and stays vectorized.

blocks.md:
This is where -O2 and -O3 differ. GCC's -O2 enables the vectorizer with `-fvect-cost-model=very-cheap`, which refuses any loop that needs a runtime alias or alignment check (an alignment check tests whether an address is a multiple of the vector size, 16 bytes here). In GCC 12 to 14 it also required the vector loop to replace the scalar loop entirely, so a loop with an unknown trip count (which needs a scalar epilogue) was refused; [GCC 15](https://gcc.gnu.org/gcc-15/changes.html) relaxed this and accepts unknown trip counts. -O3 switches to the `dynamic` model, which accepts runtime checks and epilogues. Compiling the examples with GCC 14 (`-fopt-info-vec` prints each decision):

- `add` (unknown n, no restrict): -O2 not vectorized; -O3 vectorized and "versioned for vectorization because of possible aliasing".
- `add_1024` (fixed count, restrict): vectorized at -O2.

Clang's loop vectorizer is on by default at -O2 and adds runtime pointer checks itself.

blocks.title: Instructions executed, counted from GCC's x86-64 output

scenes.caption: add_1024 (restrict pointers, 1024 ints): scalar -O1 executes 6146 instructions; -O2 and -O3 both vectorize it with SSE2 and execute 1794.

sum(a, 1000) with unknown n: GCC 14 at -O2 refuses because odd n needs a scalar epilogue, so only -O3 gets the 2-lane version: 4005 versus 2519. GCC 15 and 16 accept the epilogue but still stay scalar: their -O2 cost model rejects 2 lanes.

blocks.md:
Two related transforms show up in flag lists. **Loop unrolling** (`-funroll-loops`) copies the loop body several times per trip, so the loop makes fewer, longer trips with less counter and branch overhead. GCC's manual warns that it "makes code larger, and may or may not make it run faster", and `-fprofile-use` turns it on (lesson 7). On lesson 1's `sum`, GCC 14 with `-O2 -funroll-loops` unrolled 8 times: 11 instructions per 8 elements instead of 4 per element, after first jumping into the middle of the copies to handle the n mod 8 leftover elements.

**SLP vectorization** (superword-level parallelism) needs no loop at all: LLVM's docs describe it as combining similar independent instructions into vector instructions. GCC calls it basic-block vectorization, `-ftree-slp-vectorize`, on at -O2. With `restrict` pointers, GCC 14 -O2 turns `a[0] = b[0] + c[0];` through `a[3] = b[3] + c[3];` into one movdqu, movdqu, paddd, movups sequence, where -O1 emits 12 scalar instructions. Without restrict, a store to a[0] might change b[1], so -O2 keeps all 12.

blocks.title: sum over 8 elements: rolled loop versus 8x unrolled (GCC 14)

scenes.caption: Rolled -O2 loop: add the element, advance the pointer, compare, branch. 4 instructions per element, 32 for these 8.
Trip 2 does the same 4 instructions for one more element. Half of every trip is loop bookkeeping, not adding.
Unrolled 8x: eight adds at offsets 0 to 56 bytes from one pointer, then one pointer step of 64, one compare, one branch. 11 instructions for all 8 elements.

blocks.md: Why `movdqu` and not `movdqa`? Both move 16 bytes, but Intel's reference for [MOVDQA](https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/movdqa:vmovdqa32:vmovdqa64) says a memory operand must be aligned on a 16-byte boundary or a general-protection exception is raised; movdqu (u for unaligned) accepts any address. From plain pointer parameters the compiler cannot prove 16-byte alignment, so it uses the unaligned forms. For global arrays, whose placement it controls, GCC 14 -O2 compiled the same loop with the aligned forms, movdqa and movaps.

`restrict` is a promise, not a check. If you mark pointers restrict and then pass overlapping arrays, the behavior is undefined and the vectorized loop can silently compute the wrong answer shown above.

Vectorization processes several elements per instruction, but only when the compiler can prove it is safe: known trip counts and non-overlapping pointers help. -O2 in GCC vectorizes only the easy cases (no runtime checks, and before GCC 15 no epilogue); -O3 also takes loops that need runtime alias checks.

blocks.question: A loop over `float *out, const float *in` with a runtime length n is not vectorized at `gcc -O2` but is at -O3. What is the most likely reason?
options: -O2's very-cheap cost model rejects loops that need a runtime alias check
Floats can never be vectorized at -O2
blocks.explain: With runtime n and two pointers that may overlap, vectorizing needs a runtime overlap check. The very-cheap model used at -O2 refuses any runtime alias check (and, before GCC 15, any loop needing a scalar epilogue); -O3's dynamic model accepts them. restrict (plus a known trip count on GCC 14 and older) can make -O2 vectorize it.

blocks.question: Why does adding `restrict` to all three pointers let the compiler drop the runtime check?
options: restrict makes the arrays aligned to 16 bytes
restrict tells the compiler the arrays do not overlap, so stores cannot affect later loads
restrict copies the arrays before the loop
blocks.explain: The check exists only to detect overlap. restrict promises there is none, so the compiler can vectorize unconditionally. If the promise is false the program has undefined behavior.

lessons.title: Why code breaks at -O2: undefined behavior as an optimization license

blocks.md:
The prerequisite course showed that **undefined behavior** (UB) means the C standard places no requirements on what happens, and that Clang at -O2 compiles `x + 1 > x` to "return 1". This lesson is the practical side: a program that passes every test at -O0 and fails at -O2.

The compiler is usually not broken. Every pass from lesson 2 may assume the program never executes UB. If that assumption is false for your program, a perfectly legal rewrite changes what it does.

Why do compilers lean on UB at all? Chris Lattner's LLVM blog series lists what each kind buys. Because signed overflow is undefined, `X * 2 / 2` can become `X`, and a loop `for (i = 0; i <= N; ++i)` can be assumed to run exactly N + 1 times instead of possibly forever; with a wrapping `i` it could loop forever when N is the largest int. Because accessing an `int` through a `float *` is undefined, the compiler can use **type-based alias analysis** (TBAA): pointers to different types are assumed not to overlap, so loads can be hoisted and reused. The flip side is the three surprises below.

blocks.caption: An overflow check written after the fact. Run on the machine used for this course (Clang 22, arm64): -O0 printed -1, -O2 printed -2147483648, -O2 -fwrapv printed -1. The listings are x86-64 from Compiler Explorer.

blocks.title: An overflow check at -O0, -O2 and -O2 -fwrapv (Clang, x86-64)
blocks.code:
; clang 22 -O0 (trimmed)
  mov  eax, dword ptr [rbp - 8]    ; a
  add  eax, dword ptr [rbp - 12]   ; a + b
  mov  dword ptr [rbp - 16], eax   ; sum
  cmp  dword ptr [rbp - 12], 0     ; b > 0 ?
  jle  .LBB0_3
  mov  eax, dword ptr [rbp - 16]
  cmp  eax, dword ptr [rbp - 8]    ; sum < a ?
  jge  .LBB0_3
  mov  dword ptr [rbp - 4], -1     ; return -1
  jmp  .LBB0_4
; clang 22 -O2
add_or_fail:
  lea  eax, [rdi + rsi]            ; return a + b
  ret
; clang 22 -O2 -fwrapv
add_or_fail:
  lea  ecx, [rsi + rdi]            ; sum
  cmp  ecx, edi
  mov  eax, -1
  cmovge eax, ecx                  ; sum < a ? -1 : sum
  test esi, esi
  cmovle eax, ecx                  ; b <= 0 ? sum
  ret

scenes.caption: At -O0 the code does what the source says: the CPU's add wraps INT_MAX + 1 to INT_MIN, sum < a is true, and the function returns -1.
At -O2 Clang reasons: overflow is UB, so a + b never wraps; with b > 0 that makes sum > a, so sum < a is always false. The test and the -1 path are deleted.
-fwrapv defines signed overflow to wrap (two's complement), so the check is meaningful again and survives as two conditional moves.

blocks.md:
Fixes, best first:

1. Test *before* the operation, so overflow never happens: `if (b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b) return -1;`.
2. Use unsigned arithmetic where you want wraparound: the standard defines it to wrap.
3. Build with `-fwrapv`. GCC's manual says it makes signed add, subtract and multiply wrap, and that it "enables some optimizations and disables others". The Linux kernel uses the related `-fno-strict-overflow`, which GCC documents as implying `-fwrapv` and `-fwrapv-pointer`.

GCC 14 happens to keep this particular check at -O2. But write it as one expression, `if (b > 0 && a + b < a)`, and GCC folds `a + b < a` into `b < 0` already at -O0, so the check can never fire at any level.

The second license is the type rule. C lets an object be accessed only through an expression of a compatible type, with exceptions: signed and unsigned versions of a type, qualifiers like const, and character types, which may alias anything. GCC's `-fstrict-aliasing` lets the optimizer assume this, so an `int *` and a `float *` are taken never to point at the same bytes.

It is part of the -O2 bundle. `gcc -Q --help=optimizers` (GCC 14, x86-64) reports it disabled at -O0 and -O1 and enabled at -O2 and -O3.

blocks.title: UB-related GCC 14 flags by -O level (1 = enabled)

scenes.caption: Each row is a flag whose effect depends on an assumption about UB, as GCC 14 for x86-64 reports it. The full name of row 3 is -faggressive-loop-optimizations.
-fstrict-aliasing switches on at -O2. That is why the aliasing example below changes between -O1 and -O2.
-ftree-vrp (value range propagation) tracks the possible range of each value and, per the manual, removes checks it proves unnecessary, including null checks. Also from -O2.

-faggressive-loop-optimizations is reported on at every level, but it only acts where loop passes run (-O1 and up). And -fwrapv is off at every level: signed overflow is UB at -O0 too, the optimizer just rarely acts on it there.

blocks.caption: The textbook strict-aliasing violation: one object written as an int and then as a float.

blocks.prompt: What does `foo(&x, (float *)&x)` print at -O0, and at -O2?
blocks.reveal:
**-O0: 0. -O2: 1.** At -O0 the float store of 0.0 writes all-zero bits over x, and the reload of `*i` sees 0.

At -O2 GCC 14 compiles foo to `mov DWORD PTR [rdi], 1` / `mov eax, 1` / `mov DWORD PTR [rsi], 0x00000000` / `ret`: it returns the constant 1 without reloading, because under strict aliasing a float store cannot change an int. At -O1 GCC still reloads, and `-O2 -fno-strict-aliasing` reloads too. Clang 22 on the course machine printed the same: 0 at -O0, 1 at -O2, 0 with -fno-strict-aliasing.

blocks.md:
To read one type's bytes as another, copy them: `memcpy(&u, &f, sizeof u)` is always defined, and GCC 14 -O2 compiles a 4-byte float-to-unsigned memcpy into a single `movd eax, xmm0`. Reading a different union member than the one last written is also allowed in C, as GCC's manual notes. Or build with `-fno-strict-aliasing`, as the Linux kernel's Makefile does.

UBSan does not check this rule. Clang's [TypeSanitizer](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/TypeSanitizer.html) (`-fsanitize=type`, documented as brand new and still in development) does: on this example it reported `type-aliasing-violation ... WRITE of size 4 ... with type float accesses an existing object of type int` at the `*f = 0` line.

The third license: dereferencing a null pointer is undefined. GCC's `-fdelete-null-pointer-checks`, on by default on most targets per its manual, lets passes assume that a pointer already dereferenced cannot be null, so a later null check is dead code.

John Regehr's guide to UB walks through the Linux driver code that made this famous: it read `dev->priv` and only then tested `if (!dev) return;`. Either dev was null, so the read was already UB, or the test can never fire; so GCC at -O2 may delete it, which Regehr says risks "an exploitable security vulnerability". The kernel Makefile today passes `-fno-delete-null-pointer-checks`.

blocks.title: A null check after the dereference (GCC 14, x86-64)
blocks.code:
; gcc 14 -O0
get:
  push rbp
  mov  rbp, rsp
  mov  QWORD PTR [rbp-24], rdi
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-24]
  mov  eax, DWORD PTR [rax]        ; v = *p
  mov  DWORD PTR [rbp-4], eax
  cmp  QWORD PTR [rbp-24], 0       ; p == 0 ?
  jne  .L2
  mov  eax, -1                     ; return -1
  jmp  .L3
.L2:
  mov  eax, DWORD PTR [rbp-4]
.L3:
  pop  rbp
  ret
; gcc 14 -O1 and -O2
get:
  mov  eax, DWORD PTR [rdi]        ; return *p
  ret
; gcc 14 -O2 -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks
get:
  mov  eax, DWORD PTR [rdi]
  test rdi, rdi
  je   .L5
  ret
.L5:
  mov  eax, -1
  ret

scenes.caption: Source: int v = *p; if (p == 0) return -1; return v;. At -O0 GCC loads *p first, then compares p with 0, exactly in source order.
At -O1 and above the check is gone. If p were null, *p was already UB, so the compiler may assume p != 0 and the -1 branch is dead.
With -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks the test comes back, after the load. This is the kernel's setting.

blocks.md:
A method for "works at -O0, breaks at -O2":

1. Rebuild at the failing level with `-fsanitize=undefined,address` and run the failing input. For `add_or_fail` UBSan printed `runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'` with file and line.
2. Try the semantic switches one at a time: `-fwrapv`, `-fno-strict-aliasing`, `-fno-delete-null-pointer-checks`. If one makes the bug vanish, you know which rule the code breaks.
3. Otherwise bisect: keep -O2 and add `-fno-<flag>` for flags from `gcc -Q --help=optimizers -O2`, half the list at a time, until one flag flips the result.

Then fix the source, not the flags. Lesson 4's `restrict` is the same bargain made by hand, and lesson 6 warns that LTO, by inlining across files, gives these rewrites more to work with.

Misconception: "it works at -O0, so -O2 has a compiler bug." Compiler bugs exist, but UB in the program is far more common. And -O0 is no safe harbor: GCC folds `a + b < a` to `b < 0` even at -O0, and the next compiler version may exploit UB that this one ignores.

The optimizer assumes the program has no UB: signed overflow never happens, differently typed pointers never alias, dereferenced pointers are not null. Code that breaks those rules can change behavior at -O2. Find it with sanitizers and the -fwrapv, -fno-strict-aliasing and -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks switches, then fix the code.

blocks.question: A hash function multiplies `int h` by a large constant and relies on it wrapping. At -O2 a later check on h behaves strangely. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Make h unsigned: unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap
blocks.explain: Signed overflow is UB at every level, so -O0 only hides it and a later compiler may break it again. volatile changes memory access, not arithmetic rules. Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2 to the bit width, which is exactly what a hash wants.

blocks.question: Code reads a float's bits with `*(unsigned *)&f`. After moving to -O2 it sometimes sees stale values. Which change is correct C at every level?
blocks.explain: Accessing a float object through an unsigned lvalue breaks the type rule, so strict aliasing lets -O2 reorder or drop the accesses. memcpy copies bytes, which is always defined, and compiles to a single register move. Changing the integer type changes nothing; -O1 only hides the bug.

blocks.question: Why may GCC delete `if (!dev) return;` when it comes right after `x = dev->priv;`?
options: GCC predicts the branch is rarely taken
If dev were null, the earlier dereference was already UB, so the compiler may assume dev is not null
dev is a function parameter, so it cannot be null
blocks.explain: This is Regehr's case analysis. Either dev is null, and the dereference was UB so nothing is required, or it is not null and the check never fires. Either way the check does nothing in a program without UB, so it is dead code. Branch prediction only affects layout, never correctness.

lessons.title: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files

blocks.md:
Lesson 3 showed a call the compiler could not inline because the callee lived in another .c file. That is the normal state of a C program: each file is compiled alone into a .o, and the linker only glues machine code together. No interprocedural optimization (one that uses facts from several functions at once, like inlining) crosses a file boundary.

**Link-time optimization (LTO)** moves the optimizer to link time, when every file is available.

blocks.code:
# without LTO
gcc -O2 -c sq.c -o sq.o
gcc -O2 -c main2.c -o main2.o
gcc -O2 sq.o main2.o -o nolto

# with LTO: -flto and -O2 at compile AND link time
gcc -O2 -flto -c sq.c -o sq.o
gcc -O2 -flto -c main2.c -o main2.o
gcc -O2 -flto sq.o main2.o -o lto
blocks.caption: The square example split into two files. main2.c has int main(void) { return f(); } with f calling square(7) + 1.

blocks.prompt: Disassemble `main` in both binaries (`objdump -d`). The non-LTO main is `sub rsp, 8; mov edi, 7; call square; add rsp, 8; add eax, 1; ret`. What does the LTO main look like?
blocks.reveal: Two instructions: `mov eax, 0x32` then `ret`. 0x32 is 50. At link time GCC saw both bodies, inlined square into f and f into main, and folded the constant, exactly as in lesson 3. `nm`, which lists the symbols (the named functions and variables) in a binary, no longer shows `square` or `f` in the LTO binary at all.

blocks.md: GCC's way of doing this is called WHOPR, short for whole program optimizer. With `-flto`, each compile writes GCC's IR, the GIMPLE you met in lesson 2, into the .o instead of only machine code. It goes into special sections, named regions of an ELF file (ELF is the Executable and Linkable Format that Linux uses for object files and programs). Next to it the compile stores a **call graph**, the record of which function calls which, and a **summary** per function: compact facts such as its size and what it calls. At link time the gcc command, a driver that runs the other tools, starts lto1, GCC's link-time compiler. GCC's internals manual names three stages: local generation (LGEN) at compile time, then whole program analysis (WPA) and local transformations (LTRANS) at link time.

blocks.title: GCC link-time optimization in WHOPR mode

nodes.label:
WPA: whole call graph
inline + partition

scenes.caption: Compile step (LGEN, parallel per file): with -flto, GCC writes its internal representation GIMPLE into special ELF sections of each .o instead of, or as well as, machine code.

Link step: GCC's driver sees LTO sections and runs lto1. WPA (whole program analysis) reads the call graph and summaries of every file and makes global decisions, such as inlining square from bar.o into main in foo.o.
WPA is sequential. It splits the program into partitions of roughly equal size, minimizing references that cross between them, and writes them out with its decisions.
LTRANS runs the partitions in parallel, applies the decisions and generates machine code. The linker then produces the final binary as usual.

blocks.md:
Some practical rules from GCC's manual:

- Pass `-flto` and the same `-O` options at compile time **and** at link time. An `-O` given only at link time is largely ineffective, because early passes and the summaries they produce run at compile time.
- LTO objects are *slim* by default (GIMPLE only), so `ar` (which packs .o files into a static library) and `nm` must understand them; use `gcc-ar` and `gcc-nm`, or `-ffat-lto-objects` to also store normal machine code.
- With fat objects a misconfigured build silently links the machine code and LTO is quietly skipped.

LLVM's full (monolithic) LTO merges the whole program into one module (in LLVM a module is the IR of one source file) in one compiler process, which costs a lot of memory and time for big programs and redoes everything after any edit. GCC's default WHOPR mode above already runs LTRANS in parallel, but its WPA step still reads the whole program. LLVM's **ThinLTO** keeps the cross-module benefits without that. Per the Clang docs, each compile emits bitcode (LLVM's IR saved in a binary file) plus a compact **summary**. The link step reads only the summaries, merges them into a combined index, and decides which functions each module should import (copy in from another module so they can be inlined there). The modules are then optimized in fully parallel backends (one job per module that optimizes it and generates its machine code), by default one thread per core. A cache lets incremental builds skip unchanged modules. Usage: `clang -flto=thin -O2` at compile and link.

blocks.title: Monolithic LTO versus ThinLTO on 4 modules (toy model)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: compiling each file takes 2 units and optimizing each module takes 2. Monolithic LTO merges all modules into one and optimizes it on one core: 2 + 4 x 2 = 10 units, and all of it repeats after any edit.

ThinLTO: each compile also writes a small summary. A fast serial thin link merges only summaries (1 unit), then four backends optimize in parallel, each importing the few functions it needs (assumed 0.5 extra): 2 + 1 + 2.5 = 5.5 units.
Incremental rebuild after editing m2 with the ThinLTO cache on: only m2 recompiles, the thin link reruns, and only backends whose inputs changed rerun (here m2 alone); the rest come from the cache.

blocks.md: LTO can expose latent bugs. Code with undefined behavior, or with mismatched declarations of the same function in different files, may have "worked" only because the optimizer could not see across files. When LTO breaks a program, suspect the program first; lesson 5 shows how optimizers exploit UB.

Without LTO, a .c file is the optimizer's horizon. LTO stores the compiler's IR in the object files and optimizes the whole program at link time. ThinLTO does the global analysis on small summaries and the heavy work in parallel, so it scales and supports incremental builds.

blocks.question: A teammate adds `-flto` only to the final link command; all .o files were compiled without it. What happens?
options: No cross-file optimization: the .o files contain only machine code
blocks.explain: LTO works on the IR stored in object files. Objects compiled without -flto contain only machine code, so the link-time optimizer has nothing to work with. -flto (and -O) must be given at compile time too.

blocks.question: Which part of a ThinLTO build is serial?
options: The thin link that merges summaries and decides imports
blocks.explain: Compiles and backends run in parallel. Only the thin link is serial, and it is fast because it reads compact summaries rather than whole function bodies.

blocks.question: Why does monolithic LTO hurt the edit-compile-test loop on a large project?
options: Any edit forces re-optimizing the single merged module of the whole program
It cannot run on multicore machines at all
blocks.explain: Monolithic LTO merges every module into one and optimizes it as a unit, so a one-line change redoes the expensive whole-program step. ThinLTO's cache re-runs only the backends whose inputs changed.

lessons.title: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached

blocks.md: The compiler guesses a lot: which branch of an `if` is likely, which call is hot, how many times a loop runs. **Profile-guided optimization (PGO)** replaces the guesses with measurements from real runs. The Clang manual's examples: knowing a branch is taken very often improves the ordering of basic blocks (lesson 2), and knowing which functions are called often helps the inliner.

blocks.title: Profile-guided optimization: build, run, rebuild

scenes.caption: Step 1: build an instrumented binary. It contains counters on branches and calls.
Step 2: run it on representative inputs. On exit GCC's runtime writes a .gcda file per object; Clang writes .profraw files that llvm-profdata merge converts into one .profdata.
Step 3: rebuild with the profile. The compiler now knows which branches are hot, which calls are frequent and how many times loops iterate, and lays out and inlines accordingly.

blocks.md: In GCC, `-fprofile-use` also turns on optimizations that are usually only profitable with a profile, including `-funroll-loops` (loop unrolling, lesson 4), `-fpeel-loops`, `-ftracer` (duplicate code along hot paths so each path becomes one straight stretch that other passes optimize better) and `-fvpt` (value profile transformations: for example, if a division's divisor was usually one value, add a fast path for that value). GCC reports an error by default when the profile no longer matches the source. Clang can also use **sampling** profiles (the profiler interrupts the program many times a second and records where it is) from a profiler such as Linux perf, via `-fprofile-sample-use`, which avoids the instrumented build at the cost of less precise counts.

blocks.caption: A worked example. The training run classified 1,000,000 generated characters: 989,935 letters, 10,065 digits, no newlines or spaces. The profile was collected on arm64 and the same file then drove an x86-64 build with Clang 22, shown below.

blocks.title: kind() without and with a profile (Clang 22, x86-64)
blocks.code:
; clang 22 -O2, no profile
kind:
  xor  eax, eax
  cmp  edi, 10             ; newline?
  je   .LBB0_3
  lea  ecx, [rdi - 48]
  mov  eax, 1
  cmp  cl, 10              ; digit?
  jb   .LBB0_3
  xor  eax, eax
  cmp  dil, 32             ; space?
  sete al
  xor  eax, 3              ; 2 or 3, no branch
.LBB0_3:
  ret
; clang 22 -O2 -fprofile-instr-use
kind:
  cmp  edi, 10
  je   .LBB0_1
  lea  eax, [rdi - 48]
  cmp  al, 10
  jb   .LBB0_3
  cmp  dil, 32
  je   .LBB0_5
  mov  eax, 3              ; the hot path ends here
  ret
.LBB0_3:
  mov  eax, 1
  ret
.LBB0_5:
  mov  eax, 2
  ret
.LBB0_1:
  xor  eax, eax
  ret

scenes.caption: Without a profile Clang must guess. It tests newline and digit with branches, then computes 2 or 3 without a branch (sete, xor). A letter executes all 12 instructions.
With the profile Clang knows 99 percent of calls fall through all three tests. The hot path is straight-line: three not-taken branches, then mov eax, 3 and ret.
The rare results moved to the end of the function as tiny blocks, out of the hot path. The space test became a branch, because the profile says it is almost never taken.

blocks.md:
Two things changed: the **block layout** (the hot path falls straight through and the cold blocks sit at the end) and one branchless computation became a branch the profile says is predictable. The profile also feeds the inliner, as the Clang manual says; compare `-Rpass=inline` output with and without `-fprofile-instr-use` to see whether any decision changed for your code rather than assuming it did.

Expect gains in percent, not multiples: lesson 8 measures PGO on a whole program at 3 percent fewer instructions and a median about 7 percent lower, a gap small enough that only a careful benchmark on a quiet machine can confirm it.

PGO optimizes for the inputs you profiled. The Clang manual warns that code not exercised in the profile "will be optimized as if it is unimportant". Profiling only a unit-test suite or a single toy input can make the real workload slower.

Second lever: the target instruction set architecture (ISA), the set of instructions a CPU understands. By default x86-64 compilers target a generic CPU with SSE2. `-march=native` enables every instruction set extension of the machine doing the compiling, and GCC's manual warns that the result "might not run on different machines". The x86-64 psABI (the processor-specific ABI standard) defines portable middle steps: `-march=x86-64-v2`, `x86-64-v3` (which adds AVX2, 256-bit vector instructions) and `x86-64-v4`.

blocks.title: add_1024: instructions executed by target ISA (GCC)

scenes.caption: Baseline x86-64 has 128-bit SSE2 vectors: 4 ints per add, 256 iterations, 1794 instructions.
With -march=x86-64-v3 GCC uses 256-bit ymm registers and vpaddd: 8 ints per add, 128 iterations, 771 instructions. Fewer instructions, but the binary now requires AVX2.

blocks.md:
Third lever: floating-point rules. IEEE 754, the standard that defines float and double, rounds the result of every operation to the nearest value the format can hold. Because every step rounds, grouping matters: IEEE arithmetic is not associative, so $(a+b)+c$, adding a and b first, can differ from $a+(b+c)$, adding b and c first.

A float sum loop therefore cannot be split into vector lanes without changing results, and GCC's -O3 leaves it scalar. `-ffast-math` sets `-fno-math-errno` (math functions such as sqrt no longer set the C error variable errno, so sqrt can be one instruction), `-funsafe-math-optimizations` (which includes `-fassociative-math`, permission to regroup operations), `-ffinite-math-only` (assume no value is ever infinity or the special not-a-number value that 0.0 / 0.0 produces) and more. No -O level enables it except `-Ofast`.

Here is where the rounding in the next example comes from. A 32-bit float keeps 24 significant bits, so between two neighbouring powers of two it can hold only 2 to the 23 evenly spaced values. 1e8 lies between 2 to the 26 (about 67 million) and 2 to the 27 (about 134 million), so neighbouring floats there are 2 to the 26 divided by 2 to the 23, which is 8, apart. 1e8 + 1 is much closer to 1e8 than to 1e8 + 8, so it rounds back to 1e8.

blocks.title: Summing 8 floats: source order versus 4 vector lanes

scenes.caption: Source order: s = 0 + 1e8, then + 1. In 32-bit float the gap between neighbours near 1e8 is 8, so 1e8 + 1 rounds back to 1e8.
All three 1s are lost, then -1e8 brings the sum to 0, and the last three 1s survive: the strict IEEE answer is 3. This is what -O2 must produce.
With -ffast-math the compiler may reassociate into 4 lanes: lane k sums x[k] + x[k+4], giving 0, 2, 2, 2, then adds the lanes: 6. Clang -O2 printed 3; -O2 -ffast-math printed 6.

blocks.md: -ffast-math assumes no NaNs or infinities (-ffinite-math-only), so code that relies on IEEE behavior of NaNs and infinities can give incorrect results. Clang has deprecated -Ofast because an optimization flag changing the observable behavior of correct code surprises people. Enable fast-math per file or per function when you have verified the numerics, not globally.

Benchmark fairly: compare builds that differ in one flag, print the real compile command, and confirm what changed with `-fopt-info-vec` (GCC), `-Rpass=loop-vectorize` (Clang) or the assembly from `-S`. A speedup you cannot explain from the generated code is often a measurement error. Lesson 8 runs a full measurement.
PGO, -march and fast-math can each beat any -O level, but each adds a condition: representative profiles, a known target CPU, and numerics that tolerate reordering.

blocks.question: You build a CLI tool on a new workstation with `-O2 -march=native` and publish the binary for all Linux x86-64 users. What is the main risk?
options: It runs slower on older CPUs
It produces different numeric results on AMD
It may use instructions older CPUs lack, so it fails to run there
blocks.explain: -march=native enables every extension of the build machine, and GCC's manual warns the result might not run elsewhere. For a distributed binary use the default target, a psABI level like x86-64-v2 or v3 that you document, or runtime dispatch (ship several versions of the hot code and pick one at startup from the CPU's features). -mtune changes scheduling only.

blocks.question: A physics simulation's results change in the 6th digit after switching from -O3 to -Ofast. What is the most likely cause?
options: -Ofast enables -ffast-math, which allows reassociating floating-point operations
blocks.explain: -Ofast is -O3 plus -ffast-math. Reassociation (for example splitting a sum into vector lanes) changes rounding, exactly as in the 8-float example where the result went from 3 to 6. Neither answer is a bug; the strict one is what the source specifies.

blocks.question: You collect a PGO profile by running only the test suite, which mostly exercises error paths. What is likely to happen on production traffic?
options: Production gets the full PGO speedup anyway
The binary crashes on untested paths
The hot production paths may be treated as cold and optimized for size or laid out poorly
blocks.explain: PGO trusts the counts. Paths the profile never saw look cold, so they may be laid out away from hot code and inlined less. Profile with inputs that represent the real workload.

lessons.title: Measure it: benchmarking builds and an end-to-end tuning run

blocks.md:
Every speed number so far in this course was an instruction count read off a listing. Instructions are not time. A loop with fewer instructions can still be slower if it waits on memory, mispredicts branches or chains each step on the previous result. **IPC** (instructions per cycle) measures how many instructions the CPU completes per clock tick; the perf-stat manual's own examples show 0.34 and 1.36 for two different programs.

This lesson measures time on one small program, build by build, then covers the step after PGO, debugging optimized code, and the same levers in Rust.

A fair benchmark:

- Fixed input and fixed work, and check the output, so a broken build cannot look fast.
- One warm-up run, then many repetitions, alternating between the builds so slow drift hits all of them alike.
- Report the **median** and the spread, such as the **interquartile range** (IQR, the range holding the middle half of the runs), not one run or a mean dragged around by outliers.
- Keep the machine quiet and note its state: clock speed changes with load and temperature.
- Change one thing per comparison.

On Linux, `perf stat` reads the CPU's hardware counters while a command runs.

blocks.code:
# Linux: run 10 times, print each counter's mean and stddev
perf stat -r 10 ./wordfreq input.txt
# add L1 and last-level cache events (-d -d adds TLB events)
perf stat -d -r 10 ./wordfreq input.txt
# choose the events yourself
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,branch-misses ./wordfreq input.txt
blocks.caption: Per the perf-stat manual: -r repeats the command and prints average and standard deviation; the instructions line carries an insn per cycle (IPC) column, and branch-misses is shown as a percent of all branches. The TLB is the CPU's cache of address translations.

blocks.md:
The test program is a word-frequency counter in three files: `main.c` scans an 85 MB text file byte by byte, `util.c` holds the tiny per-byte helpers `is_word_byte` and `lower`, and `table.c` is a hash table (FNV-1a hash, linear probing). Small, but realistic: hot tiny functions in another file, plus a hash table in memory.

Each build ran 41 times in alternating order after a warm-up, timing only the counting phase with `clock_gettime`. The machine was an Apple M5 Pro laptop (arm64) that was also running other jobs, with Apple Clang 21. Instructions and cycles come from macOS's `/usr/bin/time -l`, which reports instructions retired and cycles elapsed; all six builds printed the same word counts.

blocks.code:
SRC="main.c table.c util.c"
clang -O0 $SRC -o wf_O0
clang -O2 $SRC -o wf_O2
clang -O3 $SRC -o wf_O3
clang -O2 -flto $SRC -o wf_O2_lto
# PGO: instrument, train on a DIFFERENT input, merge, rebuild
clang -O2 -flto -fprofile-instr-generate $SRC -o wf_inst
LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=wf.profraw ./wf_inst train.txt
xcrun llvm-profdata merge -o wf.profdata wf.profraw
clang -O2 -flto -fprofile-instr-use=wf.profdata $SRC -o wf_O2_lto_pgo
# arm64 counterpart of -march=native
clang -O2 -mcpu=native $SRC -o wf_O2_native
blocks.caption: The six builds. The training text has the same vocabulary as the measured input but different random draws, so the profile is representative without being the test itself.

blocks.title: Word counter: six builds, 41 runs each (Apple M5 Pro, Clang)

scenes.caption: Median time in ms for the counting phase. -O2 cuts 44 percent off -O0; LTO is the next big step; PGO adds a little. IQRs: -O2 310 to 451, -O2 -flto 228 to 323, so the runs overlap.
Instructions retired, in millions, for the whole process. -O2, -O3 and -mcpu=native are within 1 percent of each other: the extra options found nothing to do in this byte-at-a-time loop.
IPC times 100 (instructions per cycle). -O0 has the highest IPC, 3.37, and is still the slowest: it runs 2.4x the instructions of -O2, mostly cheap stack loads and stores.
Size of the program's code section in bytes. LTO made it smaller (1168 versus 1304) even though it inlined more; PGO grew it a little (1236).

blocks.md:
Read the gains with the compiler's own remarks, not guesses. Linking the LTO build with `-Wl,-mllvm,-pass-remarks=inline` printed remarks such as `'is_word_byte' inlined into 'main'`, `'lower' inlined into 'main'` and `'table_add' inlined into 'main'`. Without LTO each of those is a call into another file: is_word_byte for every one of the 85 million bytes, lower for every letter, table_add for every word. With the calls gone, instructions fell 25 percent. This is lesson 3's cross-file inlining problem, measured.

PGO then trimmed another 3 percent of instructions, and the median fell about 7 percent. Apply this lesson's own rule to that second number: the IQRs on this busy laptop are about 100 ms wide, so a 21 ms gap is inside the noise, and the instruction drop is the solid evidence. That size is typical: PGO gains are percents, which is exactly why they need a careful measurement to be seen at all.

blocks.prompt: In an earlier 21-run batch on the same laptop, -O2 and -O3 executed the same 3.39 billion instructions, yet their medians were 336 ms and 396 ms. Is -O3 slower here?
blocks.reveal: **No evidence of that.** The interquartile ranges were 288 to 471 ms for -O2 and 290 to 459 ms for -O3: they almost completely overlap, and the instruction counts are identical. In the 41-run batch the medians came out 366 and 370 ms. The difference was noise from a busy machine. Before believing a gap, check that it is larger than the spread, repeat the experiment, and look for a mechanism (different instructions, cache misses, a remark) that explains it.

blocks.md: After PGO comes **post-link optimization**. LLVM's BOLT describes itself as "a post-link optimizer developed to speed up large applications". It takes the finished binary plus a sampling profile from Linux `perf` (recorded with branch information), disassembles the functions, rebuilds their control flow, and rewrites the code layout: block order inside functions, function order, and splitting cold code away from hot code. Per its README it works on x86-64 and AArch64 ELF binaries, ideally linked with `--emit-relocs` so it can move functions. It targets large programs; a word counter whose hot code is a few hundred bytes has nothing to gain.

blocks.title: The full pipeline: PGO, then BOLT (order of steps, not to scale)

scenes.caption: PGO, as in lesson 7: build with counters, run a representative workload, merge the raw profile, rebuild with -fprofile-instr-use (here together with LTO).
BOLT: run the optimized binary under perf record with branch sampling, convert with perf2bolt, then llvm-bolt rewrites the layout of the final binary.

blocks.md:
You will also debug optimized builds. GCC allows `-g` together with `-O2`, and its manual lists what to expect: some variables you declared may not exist at all, control may jump where you did not expect, and statements may run elsewhere because they moved out of loops. The [GDB manual](https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Optimized-Code.html) says the same from the debugger's side, and GDB prints values it cannot recover as `<optimized out>`.

For a debugging build GCC suggests `-Og` with `-g`, which can debug better than -O0 because some passes that collect debug information do not run at all without optimization. When a bug shows only in the release build, debug that build with `-g` added rather than switching levels and losing the bug.

The same levers exist in Rust, because rustc generates LLVM IR. Cargo profiles set them in `Cargo.toml`:

- `opt-level`: 0, 1, 2, 3, "s" or "z"; the release profile defaults to 3. The Cargo book itself warns of "surprising results, such as level 3 being slower than 2".
- `lto`: the default `false` still does "thin local LTO" across the crate's own codegen units; `"thin"` and `"fat"` (or `true`) work across all crates in the dependency graph.
- `codegen-units`: how many pieces a crate is split into for parallel compilation, 16 by default for release; more units "may produce slower code", so `codegen-units = 1` gives LLVM the whole crate at once.

For the next step the Cargo book points to rustc's own profile-guided optimization support.

Misconception: "fewer instructions or higher IPC means faster." Here -O0 had the best IPC and the worst time, and -O2 versus -O3 showed a 60 ms median gap with identical instructions. Time is the result; instructions, IPC and cache misses are clues that explain it.

Measure time with repetitions, medians and spreads, on representative input, one change at a time. Explain each gain with counters and compiler remarks. On this program LTO gave the big win, PGO a few percent, and -O3 and -mcpu=native nothing measurable.

blocks.question: Build A: median 250 ms, IQR 215 to 330. Build B: median 262 ms, IQR 220 to 345. 41 runs each on a busy laptop. What should you conclude?
options: The runs overlap heavily: no demonstrated difference. Re-measure on a quiet machine or look for a mechanism
A is 5 percent faster; ship it
B is faster because its IQR is wider
Benchmarks on laptops are meaningless, so pick the smaller binary
blocks.explain: A 12 ms gap inside spreads of more than 100 ms is not evidence. A quieter machine, more runs, or a counter difference (instructions, cache misses) that explains the gap would make it believable. A wider IQR means more noise, not more speed.

blocks.question: A Rust service is slower than the C version built with -O2 -flto. Which Cargo release-profile change is the closest match to that C build's cross-file optimization?
blocks.explain: The default lto = false only optimizes across the crate's own codegen units. "fat" or "thin" LTO works across all crates, like -flto across all .c files, and one codegen unit lets LLVM see the whole crate at once. opt-level "z" optimizes for size, and debug info does not speed anything up.
